turn_text: Power of Care leadership, podcast, and video series. Larry Moleterno, CEO of Meridian Healthcare, asked leaders who demonstrate the power of care in their work and personal life to answer eight questions in eight minutes so you can compare their wisdom, strategy, and insights.

Welcome to Power of Care leadership. I'm pretty sure you know or you've heard of our next leader. And I think you'll find the answers to his questions very insightful and interesting. Okay, here's the first question. How does your organization or your work make your community a better place to live?

Well, it's the job of the United States Senate to pass legislation and provide oversight at the federal level to help the American people. It's really that simple. It's a noble mission that sometimes senators lose sight of. I try to stay focused on that mission. And we've had some real success. For example, one of the top priorities of mine in the Senate has been to take on the addiction crisis. It has impacted so many communities in Ohio and in the Mahoning Valley, including in Boardman. Our Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act is the first federal law to provide funding not just for proven evidence-based treatment programs, but also for the job of longer-term recovery, taking the unprecedented step of providing federal resources to support these recovery programs that have saved thousands of lives and permanently changed so many others for the better. In short, I think the job as a senator to ensure the federal government is responding to the needs of constituents, using taxpayer dollars wisely to help make our communities stronger and healthier.

turn_text: Question number two, what would people be surprised to learn about your organization or work?

Well, I think a lot of people would be surprised to know that with all the partisan gridlock you hear about and read about, it is possible to get things done in the United States Congress. Fifty-nine of our bills, as an example, have been signed into law in the Trump administration, and we had 68 of our bills signed into law by President Obama. Personal relationships matter in the Senate, and oftentimes they're the key to getting critical legislation passed. I've been fortunate to have developed good relationships with both my fellow Republicans and my Democratic colleagues. I've been consistently ranked as one of the most bipartisan senators, which I think is key to getting legislation done.
Question number three, what would people be surprised to learn about you?

Maybe one thing is that even at my age, I'm still an avid kayaker, both here in Ohio and in places like the Cuyahoga Valley National Park in Northeast Ohio and elsewhere. Back in college, in fact, I was part of the first group to ever kayak, source to see for 1900 miles along the Rio Grande River. The kayak I used, by the way, on that trip is now hanging in my conference room in DC. And the one kayak I use today, I actually keep at the Senate gym to practice rolling over in the gym pool.
Here's the fourth question. What makes you feel good about the future?

Well, this may be cliché to say, but our young people are the future. They're the hope we have. I've got a really active college internship program in our office. I was an intern myself and I believe in it. We've had over 400 young people come through our office in the past decade. And I've gotten to know most of them. Whenever I have a chance to meet with students from Ohio, whether they're interns for me, or whether they're high school, career and technical students, or whether it's my own children and their friends, I almost always come away so impressed by how engaged they are in working to make the world a better place. A lot of them have that focus. Look, we face a lot of challenges right now, but I have faith that the next generation of leaders in our country are going to work to help ensure we stay on the right path into the future. So that encourages me.

turn_text: Question number five, what most concerns you about the world today?

Well, at this very moment, I think we're all right to be concerned about the ongoing impact of COVID-19. It's a global pandemic. It's posed unprecedented challenges to our healthcare system here in this country, but also to our economy. I'm hopeful Congress can come together and get another coronavirus response package passed as we have four or five times already because it's essential that the federal government continue to invest in addressing this pandemic head on. If we don't, then the economic crisis and the healthcare crisis will be worse and it'll be even more costly.
Question number six, what would make our world a better place to live?

Our communities and our world thrive when people invest their energy into making it a better place, you know, being involved, getting engaged in your community. This is something we can all do. You can volunteer at a local charity, spend time helping a neighbor, give blood, or just do random acts of kindness, as they say. There's so many little actions people can take that add up to affecting real positive change for all of us.
Here's the seventh question. What practical advice would you give to a young person just entering the workforce today?

I guess my advice would be follow your dream, not somebody else's. You're going to be more inclined to pour all of your passion and your energy into something that you actually love and want to be involved with. And don't be afraid to try new things and see what sticks. Maybe most importantly, there's no substitute for hard work. I've found that the harder I work, the luckier I get.
And
here's the last question. What personal message or favorite quote would you put on a billboard for everyone to see?

Well when I'm asked to speak at commencement addresses for graduates, I share with students an old Portman family motto. My grandfather used to sign all his notes to me with the words, be ever kind and true. In our house we shorten it to be cat, be ever kind and true. Look, so much of succeeding in life is based on relationships and those have to be built on trust. and kindness. And honesty matters every single day and every single thing you do. So I think that's as true in a family as it is in a business. And I think it's as true on the hospital floor as it is on the Senate floor. So my advice would be be every kind and true.
